title: Leather Cutting Troubleshooting
excerpt: Leather is a flexible and heat-sensitive material that requires careful control during laser cutting. While laser processing can create precise shapes and clean edges, improper set
body_text:
¶ Leather Cutting Troubleshooting
¶ Overview
Leather is a flexible and heat-sensitive material that requires careful control during laser cutting. While laser processing can create precise shapes and clean edges, improper settings, unsuitable materials, or insufficient machine preparation may result in problems such as excessive burning, incomplete cutting, deformation, and inconsistent results.
Because leather varies significantly depending on animal source, tanning method, thickness, dye, and surface coating, the same laser parameters may not work for every material.
This guide explains common leather laser cutting problems, their possible causes, and recommended solutions.
¶ Problem 1: Leather Does Not Cut Through Completely
¶ Possible Causes
Laser power is too low.
Cutting speed is too high.
Focus position is incorrect.
Leather thickness varies.
The lens or mirrors are contaminated.
The material density is higher than expected.
The leather contains coatings that reduce laser penetration.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Increase laser power gradually.
Reduce cutting speed.
Verify the focus distance.
Clean optical components.
Perform test cuts on the actual leather batch.
Check whether the material composition is suitable for laser processing.
For thick leather, multiple passes may produce better results than excessive power in a single pass.
¶ Problem 2: Leather Edges Are Too Dark or Burned
¶ Possible Causes
Laser power is too high.
Cutting speed is too slow.
Excessive heat accumulation.
Air Assist is insufficient.
Exhaust airflow is inadequate.
The material contains oils or coatings that increase burning.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Reduce laser power.
Increase cutting speed.
Improve Air Assist airflow.
Verify exhaust performance.
Clean the lens and mirrors.
Test different settings on scrap material.
A slightly darkened edge is normal for leather because organic fibers carbonize during laser processing. Excessive burning usually indicates excessive heat input.
¶ Problem 3: Cut Edges Become Hard or Brittle
¶ Possible Causes
Excessive laser energy.
Slow cutting speed.
Multiple passes creating too much heat.
Leather contains a high amount of oil or coating.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Reduce power and increase speed.
Avoid unnecessary repeated passes.
Optimize cutting parameters for the specific leather type.
Use lower energy settings for soft leather.
Excessive heat can change the natural properties of leather and reduce flexibility.
¶ Problem 4: Leather Warps, Curls, or Shrinks After Cutting
¶ Possible Causes
Heat accumulation during cutting.
Material is too thin or lightweight.
Leather contains moisture.
The material is not properly secured.
Airflow moves the material during processing.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Reduce laser energy.
Increase cutting speed.
Secure the leather properly.
Use a vacuum table or low-tack masking when appropriate.
Store leather in a stable environment before processing.
Thin leather is especially sensitive to heat and should be tested carefully.
¶ Problem 5: PU Leather Melts or Leaves Sticky Residue
¶ Possible Causes
Synthetic coating reacts poorly to laser heat.
Laser power is too high.
Cutting speed is too slow.
The material contains unsuitable polymers.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Verify the PU leather composition.
Reduce laser power.
Increase cutting speed.
Improve exhaust airflow.
Test another material sample.
Some synthetic leather products are not suitable for laser processing due to their coating composition.
¶ Problem 6: Strong Smoke or Unpleasant Odor During Cutting
¶ Possible Causes
Leather contains dyes, oils, or tanning chemicals.
Synthetic coatings release additional fumes.
Exhaust airflow is insufficient.
Air Assist is inadequate.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Verify the material composition.
Improve ventilation.
Increase exhaust efficiency.
Maintain proper Air Assist.
Avoid processing unknown synthetic leather.
Warning
Materials containing PVC or unknown chemical coatings should not be laser processed without verification.
¶ Problem 7: Cutting Lines Are Uneven
¶ Possible Causes
Leather surface is not flat.
Material moves during processing.
Focus distance changes across the cutting area.
The laser beam is not aligned correctly.
The cutting table is uneven.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Flatten the material before cutting.
Use appropriate fixation methods.
Check focus consistency.
Verify machine alignment.
Confirm that the work surface is level.
Flexible materials require better preparation than rigid sheets.
¶ Problem 8: Small Details Are Not Cut Correctly
¶ Possible Causes
Cutting speed is too high.
Laser spot size is too large.
Excessive heat affects small features.
The material moves during processing.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Use a shorter focal length lens when appropriate.
Reduce cutting speed for detailed areas.
Optimize power settings.
Secure the material more effectively.
For complex leather patterns, accurate focus and stable material positioning are especially important.
¶ Problem 9: Smoke Stains Appear Around Cut Areas
¶ Possible Causes
Weak exhaust airflow.
Insufficient Air Assist.
Excessive laser power.
Leather surface absorbs smoke residue.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Improve exhaust performance.
Adjust Air Assist.
Reduce laser energy.
Use protective masking when suitable.
Clean the surface carefully after processing.
Light-colored leather is usually more sensitive to smoke staining.
¶ Problem 10: Different Areas of the Same Leather Sheet Cut Differently
¶ Possible Causes
Natural variation in leather structure.
Uneven thickness.
Different moisture levels.
Different surface treatments.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Measure material thickness before production.
Perform test cuts in different areas.
Sort leather pieces by similar characteristics.
Adjust production methods for natural material variation.
Unlike manufactured sheets, genuine leather naturally contains variations.
¶ Problem 11: The Cutting Quality Suddenly Becomes Worse
¶ Possible Causes
Dirty lens or mirrors.
Reduced laser power output.
Blocked Air Assist nozzle.
Poor exhaust performance.
Incorrect focus after changing materials.
¶ Recommended Solutions
Check the following:
Clean optical components.
Confirm laser power output.
Inspect Air Assist operation.
Check exhaust airflow.
Reconfirm focus position.
Always check machine condition before changing processing parameters.
¶ Quick Troubleshooting Checklist
Before adjusting parameters, verify:
Is the leather suitable for laser processing?
Is the material composition confirmed?
Is the leather flat and properly fixed?
Is the focus correct?
Are the lens and mirrors clean?
Is Air Assist working properly?
Is exhaust airflow sufficient?
Has a test cut been performed?
A systematic inspection can solve most leather cutting problems quickly.
¶ Summary
Most leather laser cutting issues are caused by excessive heat, unsuitable material selection, insufficient preparation, or incorrect machine settings.
Because leather varies significantly between different types and suppliers, parameter optimization and material testing are essential.
By controlling heat input, securing flexible materials properly, maintaining clean optics, and selecting suitable leather, users can achieve consistent cutting quality while preserving the natural appearance and performance of the material.
¶ See Also
Leather Selection Guide
Leather Laser Cutting Best Practices
Leather Laser Engraving Best Practices
Air Assist Guide
Laser Lens Selection Guide
¶ Frequently Asked Questions
¶ Why are my leather edges black after laser cutting?
A dark edge is a normal result of carbonization during laser processing. Excessive blackening usually indicates too much heat input.
¶ Why does my leather curl after laser cutting?
Curling is usually caused by excessive heat, thin material, moisture, or insufficient fixation. Reducing energy input and securing the material can help.
¶ Can all PU leather be laser cut?
No. PU leather varies greatly depending on its coating composition. Always test the material before production.
¶ Why does leather smell stronger than wood when laser cut?
Leather contains natural fibers, oils, dyes, and tanning compounds that release odors when heated. Effective exhaust ventilation is required.
¶ What should I check first when leather cutting quality decreases?
Check the lens, focus, Air Assist, exhaust system, and material fixation before changing laser parameters.

title: Leather Laser Engraving Best Practices
excerpt: Leather engraving is one of the most popular applications of laser processing because it allows users to create personalized designs, logos, patterns, text, and decorative details
body_text:
¶ Leather Laser Engraving Best Practices
¶ Overview
Leather engraving is one of the most popular applications of laser processing because it allows users to create personalized designs, logos, patterns, text, and decorative details while preserving the natural appearance of the material.
Unlike laser cutting, engraving does not separate the material. Instead, the laser removes or modifies the surface layer of leather to create visible contrast through changes in texture, color, and surface structure.
However, leather is a natural and highly variable material. The engraving result depends on leather type, tanning method, surface coating, color, thickness, and moisture content.
This guide explains best practices for laser engraving leather and provides recommendations for achieving clear, consistent, and professional engraving results.
¶ How Laser Engraving Works on Leather
Leather is mainly composed of collagen fibers that react to heat from the laser beam.
During engraving:
The laser removes or modifies the surface fibers.
The treated area becomes darker due to carbonization.
The surface texture changes, creating visual contrast.
The engraved pattern becomes visible.
The final appearance depends on:
Leather composition
Surface finish
Laser energy
Processing speed
Resolution settings
Unlike acrylic or coated metals, leather engraving is highly dependent on natural material characteristics.
¶ Choosing the Right Leather for Engraving
Different leather types produce different engraving effects.
¶ Vegetable-Tanned Leather
Vegetable-tanned leather is one of the most recommended materials for laser engraving.
Advantages:
Strong engraving contrast
Natural surface
Clear details
Develops unique aging effects
Common applications:
Wallets
Notebook covers
Keychains
Handmade leather goods
¶ Full-Grain Leather
Full-grain leather retains the natural grain structure of the hide.
Engraving characteristics:
Natural texture remains visible
Results vary slightly between pieces
Premium appearance
Suitable for:
Luxury accessories
High-end customization
¶ Top-Grain Leather
Top-grain leather has a more processed surface.
Advantages:
More consistent appearance
Predictable engraving results
Smooth surface
Suitable for:
Commercial products
Branding applications
¶ Suede and Nubuck Leather
Suede and nubuck have soft fiber surfaces.
Engraving considerations:
Lower contrast may occur.
Excessive heat can damage the texture.
Use careful power control.
¶ PU Leather
PU leather can create attractive engraving effects when the surface coating is suitable.
Possible effects:
Removing colored surface layers
Creating contrast patterns
Revealing underlying material
Always test PU leather because coatings vary between manufacturers.
¶ Selecting Engraving Style
Leather engraving can create different visual effects depending on laser settings.
¶ Surface Engraving
Surface engraving lightly modifies the top layer.
Characteristics:
Fine details
Minimal material removal
Suitable for logos and text
Recommended for:
Brand marks
Names
Decorative patterns
¶ Deep Engraving
Deep engraving removes more material from the surface.
Characteristics:
Stronger tactile effect
More visible texture
Higher contrast
Suitable for:
Decorative artwork
Embossing-style effects
Detailed patterns
However, excessive depth may damage leather flexibility.
¶ Optimizing Laser Power and Speed
Leather engraving requires a balance between visibility and heat control.
Too much energy may cause:
Excessive blackening
Burned appearance
Hard surface texture
Loss of natural leather feel
Too little energy may result in:
Weak contrast
Poor visibility
Incomplete surface modification
Recommended practices:
Start with lower power settings.
Increase energy gradually.
Test engraving depth on scrap material.
Keep settings consistent for repeated production.
¶ Choosing Appropriate Resolution Settings
Resolution affects engraving detail and processing time.
Higher resolution:
Advantages:
More detailed patterns
Smoother curves
Better small text reproduction
Disadvantages:
Longer processing time
More heat accumulation
Lower resolution:
Advantages:
Faster processing
Reduced heat buildup
Disadvantages:
Less detail
Rougher appearance
Choose resolution based on the design requirements rather than always using the highest setting.
¶ Preparing Artwork for Leather Engraving
Good artwork preparation improves engraving quality.
Recommended practices:
Use high-contrast graphics.
Convert images to appropriate engraving formats.
Simplify overly detailed designs.
Check small text size before production.
Test complex patterns on sample material.
For leather products, simple and clear designs often create better visual results than overly complex graphics.
¶ Engraving Text and Logos
Leather is widely used for personalized products.
For text engraving:
Recommended:
Use clear fonts.
Avoid extremely thin lines.
Confirm minimum readable size.
Test spacing between characters.
For logos:
Consider:
Surface texture
Design complexity
Required engraving depth
Final product usage
A logo for a wallet may require different settings from a logo on a leather belt.
¶ Managing Heat During Engraving
Heat control is one of the most important factors in leather engraving.
Excessive heat can cause:
Burn marks
Warped surfaces
Strong odors
Reduced flexibility
To control heat:
Avoid unnecessary high power.
Use appropriate speed.
Allow cooling time for repeated engraving.
Maintain clean optics.
Use suitable Air Assist.
¶ Using Air Assist During Engraving
Air Assist helps remove smoke and protect the optical system.
Benefits:
Cleaner engraving surface
Reduced smoke staining
Better lens protection
However, excessive airflow may affect loose fibers or lightweight leather.
Use airflow appropriate for the material.
¶ Engraving Coated Leather
Some leather products have painted or coated surfaces.
Laser engraving may:
Remove the surface coating.
Reveal a different color underneath.
Create contrast effects.
Before production:
Confirm coating composition.
Test engraving depth.
Check whether residue remains on the surface.
Unknown coatings should not be processed without verification.
¶ Cleaning After Engraving
After engraving:
Remove loose carbon residue.
Use a soft brush or cloth.
Avoid aggressive cleaning chemicals.
Test cleaning methods first.
Natural leather can absorb cleaning agents and change appearance.
¶ Common Applications
Leather engraving is widely used for:
¶ Personalized Products
Examples:
Names
Initials
Dates
Messages
¶ Brand Customization
Examples:
Logos
Labels
Product identification
¶ Decorative Design
Examples:
Patterns
Illustrations
Artistic textures
¶ Handmade Leather Goods
Examples:
Wallets
Covers
Keychains
Accessories
¶ Machine Maintenance After Leather Engraving
Leather engraving produces smoke containing:
Carbon particles
Oils
Dyes
Organic compounds
Regular maintenance includes:
Cleaning the lens.
Inspecting mirrors.
Cleaning the work area.
Checking exhaust performance.
Clean optics are essential for maintaining consistent engraving quality.
¶ Safety Recommendations
During leather engraving:
Always use effective exhaust ventilation.
Confirm material composition.
Avoid unknown synthetic coatings.
Keep the machine clean.
Never leave the laser unattended.
Material verification is especially important when engraving synthetic leather.
¶ Summary
Leather engraving is a valuable laser application that enables detailed customization and premium product personalization.
The best results come from selecting suitable leather, controlling laser energy, optimizing resolution, and balancing engraving depth with surface quality.
Because leather varies naturally, successful production requires testing and adjustment for each material type. With proper preparation and parameter control, laser engraving can create durable, high-quality designs while preserving the unique characteristics of leather.
¶ See Also
Leather Selection Guide
Leather Laser Cutting Best Practices
Leather Cutting Troubleshooting
Laser Engraving Guide
Air Assist Guide
¶ Frequently Asked Questions
¶ What leather is best for laser engraving?
Vegetable-tanned leather is one of the most popular choices because it produces strong contrast and clear engraving details.
¶ Why is my leather engraving too dark?
Excessive laser power or slow engraving speed can create too much heat, causing over-burning and reducing surface detail.
¶ Can PU leather be engraved?
Some PU leather products can be engraved, especially those with suitable coatings. Always test the material before production.
¶ What resolution should I use for leather engraving?
The ideal resolution depends on the design. High-detail artwork requires higher resolution, while simple logos can often use lower settings.
¶ Why does engraved leather smell after processing?
The smell comes from heated organic fibers, dyes, oils, and tanning compounds. Effective exhaust ventilation helps remove odors.

title: Fix Z-Axis Only Moving Down After Autofocus Damage
excerpt: If your autofocus assembly has been physically damaged and you are relying on manual focusing while waiting for replacement parts, you may find that the Z-axis bed refuses to move
body_text:
¶ Autofocus Damaged: Z-Axis Only Moves Downward, Cannot Move Upward During Manual Focus - Hydra Series
If your autofocus assembly has been physically damaged and you are relying on manual focusing while waiting for replacement parts, you may find that the Z-axis bed refuses to move upward. This guide explains why your laser's safety logic locks out upward movement and provides a step-by-step wiring bypass to temporarily restore manual Z-axis control.
¶ Problem Description
The autofocus assembly is damaged. While waiting for replacement parts, manual focusing must be used. However, when adjusting the Z-axis height using the control panel, the bed can only move downward and refuses to move upward.
¶ Cause
Under the motherboard's built-in safety logic, a damaged or disconnected autofocus sensor continuously reports a "triggered" status. Because the controller assumes the autofocus sensor is actively tripped (indicating the material is already touching the focus head), it locks out all upward Z-axis movement to prevent a collision with the laser head.
¶ Solution
To manually restore upward Z-axis movement:
Locate the two wires running from the motherboard to the autofocus sensor ---- the yellow-green wire and the black wire.
Short-circuit these two wires together. This signals a closed state to the motherboard, bypassing the lock and restoring upward control.
⚠️ Safety Warning
Overriding the Z-axis safety limitation removes collision protection. Exercise extreme caution when moving the platform upward manually to prevent the bed or material from crashing into the laser head, which can cause component damage or even bend the X-axis guide rail.
Important Reminder:
If these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on ZOHO: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket. A technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

body_text:
¶ Leather Selection Guide
¶ Overview
Leather is a popular material for laser cutting and engraving due to its unique texture, durability, and natural appearance. It is widely used in custom accessories, wallets, handbags, shoes, labels, patches, ornaments, and personalized products.
However, leather is not a single material category. Different types of leather vary significantly in composition, thickness, surface treatment, and processing behavior. Natural leather, synthetic leather, and coated leather may produce completely different laser results.
Choosing the correct leather before processing is essential for achieving clean cuts, high-quality engraving, and safe operation.
This guide explains the different types of leather and provides recommendations for selecting suitable materials for laser cutting and engraving.
¶ Understanding Leather
Leather is a flexible material produced by treating animal hides through processes such as tanning, drying, and finishing.
Unlike engineered materials such as MDF or acrylic, leather has natural variations in:
Fiber structure
Thickness
Surface texture
Moisture content
Oil and dye content
These characteristics affect laser absorption, cutting speed, engraving contrast, and edge appearance.
When exposed to laser energy:
The laser heats and removes the leather fibers.
Organic materials decompose and vaporize.
The cut edge becomes darker due to carbonization.
Engraved areas develop contrast through surface modification.
Because leather is a natural material, small variations between sheets are normal.
¶ Genuine Leather vs Synthetic Leather
The first step in selecting leather is understanding whether the material is natural or synthetic.
¶ Genuine Leather
Genuine leather is made from animal hide and retains a natural fiber structure.
Common types include:
Cowhide
Sheepskin
Goatskin
Pigskin
Advantages for laser processing:
Natural texture
Premium appearance
Good engraving contrast
Suitable for custom products
Typical applications:
Wallets
Bags
Shoes
Belts
Accessories
Luxury goods
The appearance after engraving depends heavily on the tanning method and surface finish.
¶ Synthetic Leather
Synthetic leather is manufactured using polymer coatings applied to fabric or synthetic substrates.
Common types include:
PU leather
PVC leather
Microfiber leather
Advantages include:
Consistent thickness
Lower cost
Wide range of colors
Uniform appearance
However, laser compatibility depends on the chemical composition of the coating.
¶ Understanding Different Leather Types
¶ Full-Grain Leather
Full-grain leather uses the outermost layer of the hide with minimal surface modification.
Characteristics:
Natural grain pattern
High durability
Premium appearance
Unique surface variations
Laser processing results:
Strong engraving contrast
Natural texture enhancement
Slight variation between pieces
Typical applications:
Premium wallets
High-end accessories
Luxury goods
¶ Top-Grain Leather
Top-grain leather has the surface lightly corrected to remove imperfections.
Characteristics:
More uniform appearance
Smooth surface
Consistent processing results
Laser engraving usually produces predictable patterns and clean contrast.
Common applications:
Bags
Fashion accessories
Commercial products
¶ Suede and Nubuck Leather
Suede and nubuck have a soft, textured surface created by processing the inner or outer fibers of the hide.
Characteristics:
Soft texture
Matte appearance
High absorbency
Laser processing considerations:
Engraving contrast may be subtle.
Excessive heat can damage the surface texture.
Lower power settings are often preferred.
¶ PU Leather
Polyurethane (PU) leather is one of the most commonly used synthetic leathers.
Characteristics:
Flexible
Lightweight
Available in many colors
Uniform thickness
PU leather may be suitable for laser processing if the coating composition is confirmed.
Potential applications:
Fashion accessories
Decorative products
Labels
Small crafts
Always verify the manufacturer's material specifications before processing.
¶ PVC Leather
Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) leather is a synthetic leather containing PVC coatings.
PVC leather is generally not recommended for laser processing.
During laser cutting, PVC may release:
Hydrogen chloride gas
Corrosive fumes
Harmful decomposition products
These gases may:
Damage machine components
Corrode optical systems
Create unsafe working conditions
Warning
Never laser process PVC leather unless the material has been specifically verified as laser-safe by the manufacturer.
¶ Choosing the Right Leather Thickness
Leather thickness is usually measured in millimeters or ounces.
The appropriate thickness depends on the application.
Thickness
Typical Applications
0.5–1.5 mm
Thin accessories, labels, patches
1.5–3 mm
Wallets, bags, decorative products
3–5 mm
Belts, structural components
Above 5 mm
Heavy-duty leather products
Thicker leather generally requires:
Higher laser power
Slower cutting speeds
More effective exhaust
Proper focus adjustment
¶ Surface Treatments
Leather may receive different surface finishes that affect laser results.
¶ Natural Finish
Natural leather with minimal coating usually provides:
Strong engraving contrast
Natural texture
Variable appearance
¶ Painted or Dyed Leather
Color-treated leather is widely used for decorative products.
Laser engraving can remove or modify the surface color, creating contrast.
Results depend on:
Dye type
Coating thickness
Surface finish
¶ Coated Leather
Some leather products include protective coatings.
These coatings may:
Melt during processing
Produce additional smoke
Affect engraving quality
Always test coated leather before production.
¶ Choosing Leather for Laser Engraving
For engraving applications, consider:
¶ Light-Colored Leather
Usually provides:
Strong contrast after engraving
Clear patterns
Better visibility
¶ Dark-Colored Leather
May produce less visible engraving because the surface color is already dark.
However, some finishes can create attractive tonal effects.
¶ Vegetable-Tanned Leather
Vegetable-tanned leather is widely used for laser engraving because:
It has a natural surface
Engraving creates strong contrast
It develops a unique appearance over time
It is commonly used for:
Wallets
Covers
Handmade leather goods
¶ Storage Recommendations
Proper storage helps maintain leather quality before processing.
Recommended practices:
Store leather in a dry environment.
Keep material flat to prevent deformation.
Avoid direct sunlight.
Protect surfaces from scratches.
Prevent excessive humidity exposure.
Leather that absorbs moisture may produce inconsistent cutting and engraving results.
¶ Materials to Avoid
Do not process leather products with unknown compositions.
Avoid materials containing:
PVC coatings
Unknown plastic films
Metallic coatings without verification
Chemical treatments unsuitable for laser processing
If the material composition is unknown, consult the supplier before laser processing.
¶ Summary
Leather is a versatile material for laser cutting and engraving, but successful processing depends heavily on material selection. Genuine leather, PU leather, and specialty leather products can produce excellent results when their composition is suitable for laser processing.
When selecting leather, consider the leather type, thickness, surface treatment, and chemical composition. Vegetable-tanned leather and high-quality genuine leather are often preferred for engraving, while PVC leather and unknown synthetic materials should be avoided.
Choosing the correct leather improves cutting quality, reduces processing issues, and helps create durable, professional finished products.
¶ See Also
Leather Laser Cutting Best Practices
Leather Cutting Troubleshooting
Laser Safety Guide
Air Assist Guide
Material Identification Guide
¶ Frequently Asked Questions
¶ What type of leather is best for laser engraving?
Vegetable-tanned leather and natural genuine leather are commonly preferred because they produce strong engraving contrast and a natural appearance.
¶ Can PU leather be laser cut?
Some PU leather products can be laser processed, but compatibility depends on the coating composition. Always confirm the material specifications before processing.
¶ Why should PVC leather not be laser cut?
PVC may release corrosive hydrogen chloride gas when exposed to laser energy, which can damage equipment and create safety risks.
¶ What thickness of leather is suitable for laser cutting?
Thin to medium leather (approximately 0.5–3 mm) is commonly used for laser products. Thicker leather may require higher-power CO₂ lasers and optimized settings.
¶ Why does leather smell during laser cutting?
Leather contains organic fibers, dyes, oils, and tanning compounds that decompose during laser processing. Proper exhaust ventilation is required to remove smoke and odors.

body_text:
¶ Leather Laser Cutting Best Practices
¶ Overview
Leather is a flexible and heat-sensitive material that requires careful control during laser cutting. Compared with rigid materials such as wood and acrylic, leather has greater variation in thickness, structure, moisture content, and surface treatment.
When processed correctly, laser cutting can produce clean edges, precise patterns, and high-quality components for wallets, bags, shoes, accessories, patches, and handmade leather products.
However, excessive heat, incorrect focus, unsuitable airflow, or improper material handling can easily cause problems such as burned edges, deformation, and uneven cutting.
This guide explains the recommended practices for laser cutting leather and helps users achieve consistent cutting results.
¶ Preparing Leather Before Cutting
Proper material preparation is the first step toward stable cutting performance.
Before processing:
Confirm the leather type and composition.
Measure thickness at different locations.
Flatten wrinkles or uneven areas.
Remove dust and surface contamination.
Perform a test cut on scrap material.
Unlike manufactured sheets such as acrylic or MDF, genuine leather naturally varies across different areas of the hide. Small differences in thickness and fiber structure are normal.
¶ Selecting Suitable Leather for Cutting
Different leather types behave differently under laser energy.
¶ Genuine Leather
Genuine leather is generally suitable for laser cutting.
Advantages:
Natural fiber structure
Stable cutting performance
High-quality finished appearance
Common applications:
Wallet components
Bags
Belts
Shoe parts
Accessories
¶ Vegetable-Tanned Leather
Vegetable-tanned leather is one of the most popular choices for laser cutting.
Advantages:
Consistent structure
Good edge appearance
Suitable for handmade products
Common applications:
Leather crafts
Covers
Small accessories
¶ PU Leather
PU leather may be suitable depending on its coating composition.
Before cutting:
Confirm the material specification.
Test for melting behavior.
Check whether the surface coating produces excessive residue.
¶ PVC Leather
PVC leather should generally be avoided.
During laser processing, PVC may release corrosive gases that can damage equipment and create safety risks.
Always verify synthetic leather composition before processing.
¶ Securing Leather During Cutting
Because leather is flexible, movement during processing can affect cutting accuracy.
Proper fixation helps prevent:
Misaligned patterns
Uneven cuts
Material movement
Distorted shapes
Recommended methods:
Use a vacuum table when available.
Apply low-tack masking tape.
Use magnets or clamps outside the cutting area.
Keep the material flat before processing.
Avoid excessive pressure that may leave permanent marks on soft leather.
¶ Choosing the Appropriate Lens
The correct lens selection affects cutting efficiency and edge quality.
Lens
Recommended Applications
1.5"
Thin leather and detailed cutting
2.0"
General leather cutting
2.5"
Medium-thickness leather
4.0"
Thick leather requiring greater depth of focus
Short focal length lenses provide finer cutting details, while longer focal lengths provide better cutting capability for thicker materials.
¶ Achieving Proper Focus
Accurate focus is essential for leather cutting.
A properly focused laser provides:
Narrow cutting lines
Cleaner edges
Reduced heat accumulation
More consistent results
Incorrect focus may cause:
Incomplete cuts
Excessive burning
Wider kerf
Uneven edge appearance
Because leather surfaces may not always be perfectly flat, ensure the cutting area remains within the effective focus range.
¶ Optimizing Cutting Parameters
Leather requires careful balance between laser power and cutting speed.
Excessive energy can cause:
Dark burned edges
Strong odors
Hard or brittle cut edges
Excessive smoke
Insufficient energy can cause:
Incomplete cutting
Uneven separation
Additional manual trimming
Recommended practices:
Use the lowest power that achieves complete cutting.
Increase speed when edge quality allows.
Test each new leather type before production.
Save optimized parameters for repeated jobs.
¶ Using Air Assist Correctly
Air Assist improves cutting performance by removing smoke and heat from the cutting area.
Benefits include:
Cleaner edges
Reduced smoke staining
Better cutting consistency
Protection of optical components
However, excessive airflow may affect lightweight leather.
Too much airflow can:
Move thin leather
Lift small pieces
Disturb flexible materials
Adjust airflow according to leather thickness and weight.
¶ Reducing Edge Burning
A certain amount of darkening is normal when cutting leather because organic fibers carbonize during laser processing.
To reduce excessive burning:
Avoid excessive laser power.
Maintain correct focus.
Improve exhaust airflow.
Keep optics clean.
Optimize cutting speed.
Use suitable Air Assist.
For premium products, perform test cuts to determine the best balance between cutting speed and edge appearance.
¶ Cutting Different Leather Thicknesses
¶ Thin Leather (0.5–1.5 mm)
Recommended for:
Labels
Small accessories
Decorative components
Considerations:
Use lower energy settings.
Secure material carefully.
Avoid excessive airflow.
¶ Medium Leather (1.5–3 mm)
Common applications:
Wallets
Bags
Crafts
Considerations:
Usually provides stable cutting performance.
Optimize speed and power for clean edges.
¶ Thick Leather (Above 3 mm)
Applications:
Belts
Structural components
Considerations:
Requires higher laser power.
May require slower speeds.
Longer focal length lenses may improve results.
¶ Improving Production Efficiency
For repeated leather cutting projects:
Create material-specific parameter libraries.
Arrange parts to maximize material usage.
Use consistent leather thickness.
Perform batch testing before mass production.
Record successful settings.
Because leather hides vary naturally, maintaining quality control is important for commercial production.
¶ Cleaning After Cutting
After laser cutting:
Remove loose residue gently.
Brush away carbon particles.
Avoid aggressive solvents.
Test cleaning methods on scrap material.
Natural leather may absorb chemicals easily, which can affect appearance.
¶ Machine Maintenance After Leather Cutting
Leather processing produces smoke containing:
Organic compounds
Oils
Dyes
Fine particles
Regular maintenance should include:
Cleaning the lens.
Inspecting mirrors.
Checking the nozzle.
Cleaning the cutting table.
Maintaining exhaust airflow.
Proper maintenance helps maintain stable cutting performance.
¶ Safety Recommendations
Always follow safe operating practices when processing leather.
Recommended precautions:
Use effective exhaust ventilation.
Verify synthetic leather composition.
Avoid unknown coated materials.
Never leave the machine unattended.
Maintain regular machine cleaning.
Material identification is essential before laser processing.
¶ Summary
Successful leather laser cutting depends on proper material selection, accurate focus, suitable parameters, effective Air Assist, and careful material handling.
Because leather varies significantly between suppliers and processing methods, testing and adjustment are essential for achieving consistent results.
By controlling heat input, preventing material movement, and maintaining clean machine components, users can produce high-quality leather components for both custom crafts and commercial production.
¶ See Also
Leather Selection Guide
Leather Cutting Troubleshooting
Leather Laser Engraving Best Practices
Air Assist Guide
Laser Lens Selection Guide
¶ Frequently Asked Questions
¶ What leather is best for laser cutting?
Vegetable-tanned leather and high-quality genuine leather are commonly preferred because they provide stable cutting performance and good edge appearance.
¶ Why do leather edges become black after cutting?
Leather contains organic fibers that carbonize when exposed to laser heat. A slightly darkened edge is normal.
¶ Can PU leather be laser cut?
Some PU leather can be processed, but the coating composition must be verified before cutting.
¶ Why does leather move during laser cutting?
Leather is flexible and lightweight. Proper fixation or vacuum holding helps prevent movement and improves cutting accuracy.
¶ Does thicker leather require a different lens?
Yes. Thicker leather often benefits from longer focal length lenses because they provide greater depth of focus.

title: Fix Laser Autofocus Stopping Before Material Contact
excerpt: Automatic focusing simplifies job setup, but if your laser head stops descending midway before touching the material, your focal distance will be completely off. This troubleshooti
body_text:
¶ Autofocus Fails: Laser Head Stops Lowering Before Contacting Material - X Series
Automatic focusing simplifies job setup, but if your laser head stops descending midway before touching the material, your focal distance will be completely off. This troubleshooting guide addresses why your Z-axis stops lowering prematurely—often while displaying Z: 0.000 on the control panel—and provides clear steps to resolve software parameter caps, sensor jams, and cable strain.
¶ Problem Description
The laser head stops moving downward midway before reaching the bottom limit of the lead screw, preventing autofocus from reaching its minimum height. At the same time, the control panel displays the Z-axis coordinate as already having reached 0.000.
Source: Image provided by a customer
¶ Cause
Incorrect Software Limits: The Max Travel value for the Z-axis in Machine Settings was modified.
Stuck Autofocus Sensor Trigger: The physical trigger pin inside the autofocus sensor is jammed, causing the sensor to continuously report a triggered state so the system controller assumes the head has hit its limit.
Restricted Cables or Air Tubing: Over time, the autofocus wiring harness or air assist tube has slipped out from the back of the laser head assembly. As the head travels downward, it pulls the lines taut, mechanically stopping further downward travel.
¶ Solution
¶ Step 1. Check Software Parameters
Open Machine Settings in LightBurn and expand the Z Axis Settings menu.
Verify that the Max Travel parameter is correctly set to 50. If it differs, update the value to 50, write the settings to the controller, and test again.
Source: Image provided by a customer
¶ Step 2. Inspect the Autofocus Sensor
Use your finger to gently push the central trigger block of the autofocus sensor upward and release it. Verify whether it springs back smoothly or remains jammed in the middle of the sensor housing.
¶ Step 3. Inspect Cable and Air Tube Clearance
Inspect the rear of the laser head for any pulled-tight wiring or air tubing. Gently pull a small amount of slack back into the laser head enclosure until there is sufficient strain relief and the head can move down through its full range of motion without pulling on the lines.
Source: Image provided by a customer
Important Reminder:
If these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on ZOHO: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket. A technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

title: Fix Hydra First Mirror Mount Elevation Issues

body_text:
¶ First Mirror Mount Fails to Elevate After Rotary Usage - Hydra Series
On dual-source Hydra Series machines, switching between rotary attachment usage and standard RF tube processing relies on an automated motorized mirror elevation mechanism. If the First Mirror (M1) mount remains stuck in the lowered position after disconnecting your rotary, the RF laser beam will be blocked from entering the optical path. This guide provides step-by-step instructions to restore proper mirror elevation through correct software sequencing, hardware checks, and driver verification.
¶ Problem Description
After using the rotary and processing with the RF tube again, no laser exits the laser head nozzle. Upon inspecting the first mirror assembly, the mirror mount is found stuck in the lowered position, causing the RF laser to hit and reflect directly off the machine's metal backplate.
Source: Image provided by a customer
¶ Cause
The rotary mode switch was not toggled off in the required procedural sequence after rotary operation.
Loose wiring connections or unseated plugs between the mount elevation motor, motor driver, and autofocus board.
Incorrect DIP switch settings on the motor driver.
The mirror elevation motor is damaged, or its lead screw is bent.
¶ Solution
¶ Method 1. Verify the Rotary Toggle Sequence
After using the rotary, you must exit rotary mode using the following exact sequence:
Turn the physical rotary toggle switch on the side of the machine back ON.
Open Rotary Setup in LightBurn and toggle the Enable Rotary option to OFF.
Turn the physical rotary toggle switch on the side of the machine OFF. Test the machine to see if the M1 mirror mount now elevates and functions properly.
¶ Method 2. Inspect Elevation Assembly Components
¶ Step 1. Inspect the Mirror Elevation Motor and Lead Screw
Power OFF the equipment completely. Manually rotate the motor lead screw clockwise and counterclockwise by hand. Check if the mirror mount binds, or stutters at any point along its vertical travel. If binding occurs due to a bent lead screw, the motor assembly must be replaced.
Note: If the driver and wiring pass inspection, a non-responsive mount may also indicate a damaged motor requiring replacement.
¶ Step 2. Inspect the Motor Driver
Open the lower-right access door on the back of the machine to locate the motor driver. Check the diagnostic LED indicator on the driver (a green light indicates normal operation) and verify that the DIP switches on the driver are correctly toggled to positions 7 and 8.
¶ Step 3. Check Cable and Terminal Connections
Inspect all wiring harnesses and connectors along the circuit path—from the autofocus board, motor driver to the M1 mount motor—to ensure no plugs have vibrated loose.
the autofocus board
Important Reminder:
If these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on ZOHO: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket. A technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

body_text:
¶ Fabric Selection Guide
Fabric is one of the most versatile materials used in laser processing. From personalized apparel and home décor to industrial textiles and fashion accessories, laser cutting and engraving enable precise, contact-free processing across a wide variety of fabrics.
However, not all fabrics respond to laser energy in the same way. Natural fibers, synthetic materials, and blended textiles each exhibit different cutting characteristics, engraving effects, and safety considerations. Selecting the appropriate fabric is the first step toward achieving clean edges, detailed engravings, and consistent processing results.
This guide introduces the most common fabric types, explains how they behave during laser processing, and highlights materials that should not be processed with a laser.
¶ Fabric Categories
Fabric materials can generally be divided into three groups based on their fiber composition.
¶ Natural Fabrics
Natural fabrics are made from plant or animal fibers. They typically absorb CO₂ laser energy efficiently and are widely used for engraving because they produce clear, high-contrast markings.
Common natural fabrics include:
Cotton
Linen
Denim
Canvas
Wool
¶ Characteristics
Excellent laser absorption
High engraving contrast
Slightly darkened cut edges may occur
Suitable for decorative engraving and cutting
Typical applications include:
Apparel
Tote bags
Patches
Home décor
Quilting
¶ Synthetic Fabrics
Synthetic fabrics are manufactured from thermoplastic fibers. During laser cutting, these fibers melt slightly, sealing the cut edge and helping prevent fraying.
Common synthetic fabrics include:
Polyester
Nylon
Fleece
Acrylic felt
¶ Characteristics
Smooth, sealed cutting edges
Minimal fraying
High cutting efficiency
Lower engraving contrast than natural fibers
Typical applications include:
Sportswear
Outdoor gear
Industrial textiles
Flags
Decorative felt products
¶ Blended Fabrics
Blended fabrics combine natural and synthetic fibers to balance comfort, durability, and cost.
Common blends include:
Cotton / Polyester
Linen / Polyester
Wool blends
¶ Characteristics
Laser performance depends on the fiber ratio.
For example:
Higher cotton content generally produces darker engraving.
Higher polyester content creates smoother cut edges with reduced fraying.
Whenever processing blended materials, perform a small test before production to determine the optimal laser settings.
¶ Fabric Compatibility
The following table provides a general overview of how common fabrics perform during laser cutting and engraving.

Note: Actual processing results may vary depending on fabric thickness, weave density, coatings, dyes, and machine configuration. Always perform a test on scrap material before full production.
¶ Materials to Avoid
Some fabrics should never be processed with a laser because they release hazardous gases or may damage the machine.
¶ PVC and Vinyl
PVC (Polyvinyl Chloride) and vinyl materials release hydrogen chloride gas when exposed to laser heat.
This gas can:
Damage mirrors and lenses
Corrode metal machine components
Produce toxic fumes that are hazardous to operators
These materials should never be laser cut or engraved.
¶ Unknown Coated Fabrics
Some waterproof or flame-retardant fabrics contain coatings whose chemical composition is unknown.
Potential risks include:
Toxic fumes
Excessive smoke
Sticky residues on optics
Unpredictable cutting quality
If the coating composition cannot be confirmed, avoid laser processing.
¶ Artificial Leather with PVC Base
Not all artificial leather is laser-safe.
Some synthetic leathers use PVC as the backing material, which presents the same hazards as standard PVC.
Always verify the material specifications before processing.
¶ Preparing Fabric for Laser Processing
Proper material preparation improves cutting quality and helps prevent processing issues.
Before starting, check the following:
Lay the fabric flat to eliminate wrinkles.
Secure lightweight materials with magnets, weights, or a vacuum table.
Remove dust, lint, and loose fibers from the surface.
Confirm that the material contains no PVC or unknown coatings.
Perform a small test cut or engraving to verify settings.
Taking a few minutes to prepare the material can significantly improve processing consistency and reduce waste.
¶ Choosing the Right Fabric
Different projects require different material characteristics.
For example:
Cotton is ideal for detailed engraving and personalized products.
Canvas offers excellent durability for bags, labels, and home décor.
Denim produces high-contrast decorative engravings.
Polyester is preferred when clean, sealed cutting edges are required.
Felt is widely used for crafts, ornaments, and educational products.
Selecting the appropriate fabric based on your application helps maximize both quality and production efficiency.
¶ Frequently Asked Questions
¶ 1. Can all fabrics be laser cut?
No. Most natural and synthetic fabrics can be processed safely, but PVC-based materials, vinyl, and fabrics with unknown chemical coatings should never be laser processed.
¶ 2. Why do some fabrics have brown edges after cutting?
Natural fibers such as cotton and linen may develop slight discoloration because they char instead of melting. Reducing laser power or increasing cutting speed can help minimize this effect.
¶ 3. Why doesn't polyester fray after laser cutting?
Polyester is a thermoplastic material. During cutting, the laser melts the edge slightly, creating a sealed finish that resists fraying.
¶ 4. Should I wash fabric before laser engraving?
If the fabric contains sizing agents, oils, or surface treatments, washing it beforehand can improve engraving consistency. Always ensure the fabric is completely dry before processing.
¶ 5. Can colored fabrics be laser engraved?
Yes. However, engraving results vary depending on the dye, fiber composition, and fabric color. Dark-colored fabrics often produce more subtle contrast than light-colored materials.

title: Fabric Laser Cutting Guide
excerpt: Laser cutting has become one of the most efficient methods for processing fabrics. Unlike mechanical cutting tools, a CO₂ laser cuts without physical contact, eliminating blade wea
body_text:
¶ Fabric Laser Cutting Guide
Laser cutting has become one of the most efficient methods for processing fabrics. Unlike mechanical cutting tools, a CO₂ laser cuts without physical contact, eliminating blade wear while producing intricate shapes, consistent dimensions, and clean edges.
For many synthetic fabrics, the laser also seals the cut edge during processing, reducing or eliminating fraying. This makes laser cutting ideal for applications ranging from fashion and upholstery to industrial textiles and custom crafts.
This guide explains how laser cutting works on fabric, how to prepare your machine and materials, common processing techniques, and solutions to frequently encountered cutting issues.
¶ How Laser Cutting Works on Fabric
A CO₂ laser emits infrared light at a wavelength of 10.6 μm, which is readily absorbed by most organic and polymer-based fabrics.
When the focused laser beam reaches the material surface, the fabric fibers rapidly heat up and either:
Vaporize (common with natural fibers such as cotton and linen)
Melt and separate (common with synthetic fibers such as polyester and nylon)
Because the laser never physically touches the material, there is:
No blade deformation
No mechanical pulling or distortion
High repeatability
Smooth, intricate cutting paths
For thermoplastic fabrics, the melted edge solidifies immediately after cutting, creating a sealed edge that helps prevent fraying.
¶ Choosing the Right Worktable
The worktable plays an important role in cutting quality, especially for lightweight and flexible materials.
¶ Honeycomb Table
A honeycomb table supports fabric evenly while allowing smoke and heat to escape through the openings.
Advantages include:
Good airflow
Reduced back reflections
Suitable for thin and lightweight fabrics
Common choice for general fabric cutting
¶ Knife Blade Table
A knife blade table minimizes contact between the material and the work surface.
It is often recommended for:
Thick fabrics
Heavy canvas
Multi-layer cutting
Industrial textiles
Reduced surface contact also helps minimize scorch marks on the underside of the material.
¶ Vacuum Table
A vacuum table holds lightweight fabrics flat during processing.
Benefits include:
Prevents material shifting
Improves cutting accuracy
Reduces wrinkles
Ideal for thin, lightweight, or stretchy fabrics
For production environments, vacuum tables can significantly improve consistency and reduce material waste.
¶ Preparing the Fabric
Proper preparation is essential for achieving consistent cutting results.
Before starting a job:
Remove wrinkles by flattening the fabric.
Secure lightweight materials with magnets, weights, or a vacuum table.
Ensure the material is clean and dry.
Remove loose threads or lint.
Verify that the fabric contains no PVC or unknown coatings.
Perform a small test cut before full production.
Well-prepared materials reduce cutting errors and improve edge quality.
¶ Air Assist Recommendations
Air Assist helps remove smoke and debris from the cutting area, but excessive airflow can move lightweight fabrics during processing.
General recommendations:
Use low air pressure for thin or lightweight fabrics.
Increase airflow slightly for thicker materials such as canvas or felt.
Avoid high-pressure airflow on delicate fabrics like silk or chiffon.
Keep the nozzle clean to maintain consistent airflow.
Proper Air Assist settings improve cut quality while minimizing fabric movement.

¶ Recommended Cutting Workflow
Following a consistent workflow helps improve both efficiency and repeatability.
Prepare and flatten the fabric.
Secure the material to prevent movement.
Clean the lens and mirrors if necessary.
Focus the laser according to the installed lens.
Run a framing test to verify the cutting area.
Perform a small test cut.
Adjust power and speed if required.
Start the full cutting job.
Inspect the cut edges after completion.
Developing a standard workflow also makes it easier to reproduce successful results across multiple jobs.
¶ Multi-Layer Fabric Cutting
Laser cutting multiple fabric layers can improve production efficiency, but it also increases processing complexity.
When cutting stacked materials:
Keep layer thickness consistent.
Compress the material gently to maintain focus.
Increase laser power gradually rather than dramatically.
Reduce cutting speed if lower layers are not fully separated.
Test the maximum stack height before production.
Different fabrics respond differently to multi-layer cutting, so production testing is always recommended.
¶ Common Cutting Problems
¶ Burned or Darkened Edges
Possible causes
Excessive laser power
Cutting speed too slow
Dirty optics
Poor ventilation
Solutions
Reduce power.
Increase cutting speed.
Clean the lens and mirrors.
Improve exhaust performance.
¶ Incomplete Cuts
Possible causes
Insufficient power
Incorrect focus
Thick material
Dirty optics
Solutions
Increase power slightly.
Refocus the laser.
Reduce cutting speed.
Clean the optical components.
¶ Fabric Moves During Cutting
Possible causes
Excessive Air Assist
Lightweight material
Material not secured
Solutions
Reduce Air Assist pressure.
Use magnets or weights.
Use a vacuum table if available.
¶ Melted Edges
This issue is most common with polyester and nylon.
Solutions
Reduce power.
Increase cutting speed.
Improve cooling airflow.
Test different focus positions if necessary.
¶ Safety Considerations
Always follow standard laser safety practices when cutting fabric.
Never process PVC or vinyl materials.
Keep the exhaust system operating throughout the job.
Remove lint buildup regularly to reduce fire risk.
Never leave the machine unattended during cutting.
Keep a suitable fire extinguisher nearby.
Stop processing immediately if excessive smoke or flames appear.
Although most fabrics are relatively thin, they are combustible materials and should always be monitored during laser processing.
¶ Frequently Asked Questions
¶ 1. Why does polyester have sealed edges after laser cutting?
Polyester is a thermoplastic material. The laser melts the fibers as it cuts, and the molten material solidifies immediately, creating a clean, sealed edge that resists fraying.
¶ 2. Can multiple layers of fabric be laser cut?
Yes. However, the maximum number of layers depends on the fabric type, thickness, laser power, and required edge quality. Always test before production.
¶ 3. Should Air Assist always be enabled?
Generally, yes. Low Air Assist improves smoke removal and protects the optics. However, excessive airflow may cause lightweight fabrics to shift during cutting.
¶ 4. Why is my fabric not cutting completely?
Common causes include insufficient laser power, incorrect focus, dirty optics, or excessive cutting speed. Performing a test cut is the best way to identify the correct settings.
¶ 5. Does fabric color affect laser cutting?
In most cases, fabric composition has a greater influence than color. However, dyes and surface treatments can slightly affect laser absorption and edge appearance.

title: Fabric Laser Engraving Guide
excerpt: Laser engraving offers a fast, precise, and non-contact method for adding permanent designs, logos, patterns, and text to fabric. Unlike laser cutting, which separates the material
body_text:
¶ Fabric Laser Engraving Guide
Laser engraving offers a fast, precise, and non-contact method for adding permanent designs, logos, patterns, and text to fabric. Unlike laser cutting, which separates the material, engraving removes or modifies only the surface fibers to create visible markings while preserving the overall structure of the fabric.
Depending on the fabric type and laser settings, engraving can produce subtle textures, high-contrast graphics, vintage effects, or decorative surface patterns. From personalized apparel and branded accessories to home décor and industrial labeling, laser engraving has become a versatile solution for textile customization.
This guide explains which fabrics are suitable for engraving, recommended machine settings, common applications, and practical techniques for achieving consistent, high-quality results.
¶ How Laser Engraving Works on Fabric
A CO₂ laser engraves fabric by delivering controlled heat to the material's surface. Instead of cutting completely through the fabric, the laser removes, lightens, darkens, or slightly melts the surface fibers, depending on the material composition.
Different fabrics respond differently:
Natural fibers (such as cotton, linen, and denim) often darken or char slightly, creating high-contrast engravings.
Synthetic fabrics (such as polyester and nylon) may lighten, melt slightly, or change texture.
Blended fabrics produce results that vary according to the fiber ratio.
Because engraving affects only the surface, the structural integrity of the material is generally maintained when proper settings are used.
¶ Best Fabrics for Laser Engraving
The following materials generally produce excellent engraving results.
¶ Cotton
Cotton creates sharp, high-contrast engravings and is one of the most commonly engraved fabrics.
Typical applications include:
Tote bags
T-shirts
Decorative textiles
Labels
¶ Denim
Denim is well known for its distinctive faded engraving effect.
Common uses include:
Fashion customization
Decorative artwork
Personalized apparel
Brand graphics
Laser engraving can selectively remove dye from the surface, creating detailed patterns without damaging the fabric when properly adjusted.
¶ Canvas
Canvas is durable and produces clean engravings suitable for commercial products.
Typical applications:
Bags
Storage organizers
Promotional products
Home décor
¶ Felt
Felt engraves cleanly and provides noticeable texture changes.
Typical applications:
Crafts
Holiday ornaments
Educational products
Decorative accessories
¶ Linen
Linen offers a natural appearance and subtle engraving contrast, making it suitable for decorative and home furnishing applications.
¶ Fabrics That Require Extra Care
Some fabrics are more sensitive to laser heat and require careful parameter adjustment.
These include:
Silk
Satin
Chiffon
Lightweight polyester
Stretch fabrics
For delicate materials:
Use lower laser power.
Increase engraving speed.
Perform test engravings before production.
Avoid excessive heat buildup.
¶ Recommended Starting Parameters

¶ Optimizing Engraving Quality
Achieving consistent engraving results involves more than simply adjusting power and speed.
Consider the following best practices:
Clean the fabric surface before engraving.
Ensure the material is flat and wrinkle-free.
Secure lightweight fabrics to prevent movement.
Start with lower power and increase gradually.
Test different DPI settings for the desired detail level.
Use proper ventilation to remove smoke and lint.
For detailed graphics, running several small test samples is often more efficient than adjusting settings during a full production run.
¶ Common Fabric Engraving Applications
Laser engraving is suitable for a wide range of textile products.
Popular applications include:
¶ Personalized Apparel
T-shirts
Denim jackets
Hats
Hoodies
¶ Branding
Company logos
Product labels
Fabric tags
Promotional merchandise
¶ Decorative Products
Canvas wall art
Cushion covers
Table runners
Quilting patterns
¶ Craft Projects
Felt ornaments
Seasonal decorations
Educational materials
Handmade gifts
¶ Industrial Uses
Textile identification
Production markings
Sewing guides
Alignment marks
¶ Common Engraving Problems
¶ Fabric Turns Brown or Black
Possible causes
Excessive laser power
Low engraving speed
Heat accumulation
Solutions
Reduce power.
Increase engraving speed.
Improve ventilation.
¶ Low Contrast
Possible causes
Laser power too low
Fabric not suitable for engraving
Dark-colored material
Solutions
Increase power slightly.
Test different DPI values.
Try engraving on lighter-colored fabric.
¶ Fabric Shrinks After Engraving
Possible causes
Excessive heat
Thin or delicate material
Solutions
Lower laser power.
Increase speed.
Reduce engraving density.
¶ Surface Melts
This problem usually occurs on synthetic fabrics.
Solutions
Reduce laser power.
Increase scanning speed.
Lower engraving resolution if necessary.
¶ Safety Tips
Although engraving generally uses lower power than cutting, safety remains essential.
Always remember to:
Never engrave PVC or vinyl materials.
Keep the exhaust system running during operation.
Remove accumulated lint regularly.
Monitor the engraving process continuously.
Keep optical components clean for consistent performance.
Proper ventilation helps maintain engraving quality while protecting both the operator and the laser system.
¶ Frequently Asked Questions
¶ 1. Does laser engraving weaken fabric?
When performed with appropriate settings, engraving affects only the surface fibers and typically does not significantly reduce the strength of the material. Excessive power, however, can damage the fabric.
¶ 2. Can photographs be engraved onto fabric?
Yes. Cotton, denim, canvas, and some felt materials can reproduce grayscale images effectively after proper image processing and parameter optimization.
¶ 3. Will laser engravings wash away?
No. Laser engraving permanently modifies the fabric surface rather than applying ink or dye. However, repeated washing may gradually change the appearance depending on the fabric type and engraving depth.
¶ 4. Why does denim produce a faded engraving effect?
Laser energy removes or lightens the indigo dye on the fabric surface, creating a high-contrast vintage appearance without the need for chemicals.
¶ 5. Should engraving be performed before or after cutting?
In most cases, engraving should be completed before cutting. This helps keep the material stable and reduces the risk of movement after smaller pieces have been separated.
¶ Related Articles
To learn more about laser processing fabrics, continue with the following guides:

body_text:
¶ How to Use Conveyor in Lightburn
¶ Usage — step-by-step
¶ Step 1 - Set the Parameters
After connecting the Conveyor to the machine's rotary axis port, turn ON the rotary axis switch located next to the port.
In LightBurn, open the Rotary Setup window and configure the following settings:
Rotary Type：Select Roller, and check the box to Enable Rotary.
Rotary Axis：The default selection is the Y-Axis (some machines may use the A-Axis).
Parameters：Input the numerical values found on the aluminum card that came with the unit into the parameter fields on the right side of the pop-up window.
Once configured, the Conveyor is ready to use.
If you encounter a length limitation when processing material with the Conveyor (e.g., restricted to 500 mm):
Open Machine Settings in LightBurn.
Find Max travel within the U Axis Settings.
Change this value to 10000 and Click Write.
The Conveyor needs to be turned off and disconnected, then the machine needs to be reset or restarted before the Conveyor can be reconnected to truly write the Max Travel value to the mainboard.
¶ Step 2 - Processing Settings
1. We recommend selecting User Origin for Start From and the top left corner for Job Origin. This setting can reduce the occurrence of errors.
2. The width of the graph cannot exceed the working area. Please note that it should not exceed the Max Travel of the X-axis.
¶ Step 3 - After Using the Conveyor
In LightBurn, open the Rotary Setup window and uncheck the Enable Rotary box.
Turn OFF the rotary axis switch on the machine and disconnect the Conveyor's cable.
Finally, click the Reset icon on the machine's control panel to restore the machine to its normal processing state.
Caution:
If the shutdown sequence is incorrect or if you turn off the rotary axis switch directly (skipping the LightBurn disable step), it may cause homing errors or abnormal Y-axis movement.

title: Fix No Laser Output Issue - VertiGO Series
excerpt: If your VertiGO machine's laser head moves and fans spin normally, but no laser beam hits your material during a job or manual pulse test, you are dealing with an output cut-off. T
body_text:
¶ No Laser Output During Processing or Pulse Test - VertiGO Series
If your VertiGO machine's laser head moves and fans spin normally, but no laser beam hits your material during a job or manual pulse test, you are dealing with an output cut-off. This troubleshooting guide walks you through diagnosing whether the issue stems from simple software settings, optical beam alignment, control board pre-ignition locks, or a hardware failure in the power supply or RF laser tube.
¶ Problem Description
During a processing job, the laser head moves and the fans rotate normally, but no laser beam is emitted. No marks are left on the material, and the RF tube shows zero laser output.
¶ Cause
Layer power settings in the file are configured too low.
The beam path is severely misaligned or blocked.
The equipment is still in its pre-ionization warm-up cycle.
Damaged power supply unit, damaged optical lenses, loose/damaged wiring harnesses or connectors, faulty Fan Control board port, or natural aging/failure of the RF tube.
¶ Solution
⚠️ Important Reminder
After powering on, the RF tube undergoes a pre-ionization process for up to 45 seconds. Once completed, the machine will emit three beeps, indicating that the RF tube is fully ready for operation.
¶ Method 1. Verify Layer Parameters
Check your software laser power settings to ensure the output percentage is not set too low, which can cause the machine to appear as though it is not firing.
¶ Method 2. Confirm Operating Ambient Temperature
The operating ambient temperature for the laser tube must be kept strictly between 32°F and 95°F (0°C to 35°C). Operating outside this temperature range may trigger safety cutoffs or operational anomalies, resulting in no laser output from the RF tube.
¶ Method 3. Check Direct Output at the RF Tube Aperture
Remove the rear panel of the VertiGO. Place a small piece of wood directly in front of the RF tube exit aperture. Press the Pulse button on the control panel to test for direct laser output at the source:
Laser output present: The fault is caused by beam path misalignment or optical lens damage. Proceed to Method 4 to calibrate the optical path.
No laser output: The issue lies within the RF tube itself, the wiring, or the power supply.
¶ Method 4. Inspect Lenses and Beam Alignment
Inspect all mirrors, the beam combiner, and the focus lens along the optical path. Cracks, burns, or severe physical damage to any optic will block the laser beam from traveling to the work surface.
Refer to this step-by-step alignment tutorial: How to Adjust the Optical Path In Vertigo?
¶ Method 5. Inspect the Pre-Ignition Status
If you do not hear the three beeps 45 seconds after powering on, open the rear cover and inspect the D5, D2, and D1 LED indicators on the control board:
Normal Status: Indicators D5, D2, and D1 should all be OFF.
Abnormal Status: If any LED remains lit, refer to the following diagnostic guide:
D5 (Solid ON): Indicates a voltage anomaly. Perform power/electrical troubleshooting.
D2 (Solid ON): Indicates the RF tube temperature is too high. The laser will lock out. Stop operation, wait 4–5 minutes for the RF tube to cool down, and try again.
D1 (Solid ON): Indicates the unit is still stuck in the pre-ignition phase. Wait a few extra minutes.
Locate the gray Ethernet network cable. Unplug both ends (at the Fan Control board and the RF tube) and firmly reconnect them. If the issue persists, swap it out with a known working Ethernet cable.
¶ Method 6. Inspect the Power Supply Unit
Prepare a multimeter. Locate the power supply and check whether its green LED indicator is solid ON:
Green Light Solid ON: Use multimeter probes to measure the voltage across the +V and -V terminals. It should read 48V. An abnormal reading confirms a faulty PSU.
Green Light OFF: Measure the input voltage across terminals L4 and N4. It should read 220V (or 110V). If input voltage is normal but the green light remains off, the PSU is defective. If input voltage is abnormal, check the upstream main power wiring.
¶ Method 7. Inspect Wiring and Terminal Connections
Locate the FanCtrl board. Use a multimeter to measure the voltage across the L-ON and GND terminals. It should read 5V.
With the machine powered OFF, verify that all wiring connectors on the Fan Control board are firmly seated.
Check the primary power cables (positive and negative terminals) connected to the RF tube to ensure they are securely fastened.
¶ Method 8. Isolate and Test the RF Tube
To determine whether the fault stems from the RF tube itself or an incoming control signal, perform a short-circuit diagnostic test using a standard Ethernet cable:
1. Take a spare Ethernet cable and cut off the RJ45 crystal connector at one end.
2. Strip the insulation from wires 1, 3, and 7 (Orange-White, Green-White, Brown-White) and twist them firmly together (shorted).
Note: This modified end remains free and does NOT plug into the mainboard.
3. Plug the intact RJ45 connector on the other end directly into the network port on the RF tube.
4. Power on the machine and wait 42 seconds for the pre-ignition cycle to complete.
Laser Fires Normally: The RF tube is fully functional. The issue lies within the mainboard or control signal pipeline.
No Laser Output: The RF tube is defective and requires replacement.
Important Reminder:
If these steps do not resolve the issue, please submit a support ticket on ZOHO: https://zohodesk.1laser.com/portal/en/newticket. A technician will then be able to conduct a more in-depth diagnosis and resolve your problem.

title: MDF Selection Guide
excerpt: Medium-Density Fiberboard (MDF) is one of the most commonly used engineered wood materials for laser cutting and engraving. Its smooth surface, uniform density, and consistent inte
body_text:
¶ MDF Selection Guide
¶ Overview
Medium-Density Fiberboard (MDF) is one of the most commonly used engineered wood materials for laser cutting and engraving. Its smooth surface, uniform density, and consistent internal structure make it an excellent choice for signs, decorative products, architectural models, furniture components, prototypes, and painted finished goods.
Unlike natural wood, MDF has no visible grain direction or internal voids, allowing laser systems to produce highly consistent cutting and engraving results across the entire sheet.
However, not all MDF products are manufactured the same way. Material grade, density, thickness, resin formulation, and surface finish can all influence cutting quality, smoke generation, edge appearance, and machine maintenance.
This guide explains the different types of MDF and provides recommendations for selecting the most suitable material for laser processing.
¶ Understanding MDF
Medium-Density Fiberboard (MDF) is an engineered wood product manufactured by compressing refined wood fibers with synthetic resin and wax under high temperature and pressure.
The resulting panel has a homogeneous internal structure without natural grain or veneer layers.
Compared with solid wood and plywood, MDF offers several advantages for laser processing:
Smooth, uniform surface
Consistent internal density
No wood grain direction
Predictable engraving depth
Excellent dimensional stability
Suitable for intricate cutting patterns
Because the material is manufactured rather than naturally grown, MDF generally provides more repeatable machining results than many natural wood products.
¶ How MDF Differs from Plywood
Although MDF and plywood are both engineered wood products, their construction and laser processing characteristics are significantly different.
Characteristic
MDF
Plywood
Internal Structure
Uniform wood fibers
Multiple wood veneer layers
Grain Direction
None
Visible grain in each veneer
Density
Highly consistent
Varies between layers
Surface Finish
Smooth
Natural wood texture
Engraving Appearance
Uniform
Influenced by wood grain
Internal Voids
Rare
Possible in lower-grade plywood
Dust Generation
Higher
Lower
Because MDF has a homogeneous structure, it is often preferred for projects that require smooth painted surfaces or highly consistent engraving results.
¶ Understanding MDF Grades
Different MDF grades are designed for different environments and applications. Choosing the appropriate grade improves machining quality and helps avoid unnecessary processing issues.
¶ Standard MDF
Standard MDF is the most commonly used material for laser cutting and engraving.
Characteristics include:
Uniform density
Smooth surface
Consistent engraving quality
Reliable cutting performance
Cost-effective
Widely available
Typical applications:
Decorative signs
Crafts
Architectural models
Display products
Boxes
Furniture components
For most laser applications, Standard MDF is the recommended choice.
¶ Moisture-Resistant MDF (MR MDF)
Moisture-Resistant MDF is manufactured with modified resin systems that improve stability in humid environments.
Many manufacturers identify MR MDF by its green-colored core, although color may vary.
Typical applications include:
Kitchens
Bathrooms
Indoor humid environments
Cabinetry
Compared with Standard MDF, MR MDF may:
Require slightly higher laser energy
Produce more smoke
Leave additional residue on optical components
A test cut is recommended before production.
¶ Fire-Retardant MDF (FR MDF)
Fire-Retardant MDF contains flame-retardant additives that improve fire resistance in commercial and architectural applications.
Common uses include:
Public buildings
Commercial interiors
Fire-rated construction
Although FR MDF can technically be processed by some laser systems, it is generally not recommended because flame-retardant additives may:
Reduce cutting efficiency
Produce heavier smoke
Leave additional residue
Increase optical contamination
Affect edge quality
Warning
Flame-retardant additives vary by manufacturer. Always review the material safety documentation before attempting laser processing.
¶ High-Density Fiberboard (HDF)
High-Density Fiberboard (HDF) is manufactured using finer wood fibers compressed at higher pressure than Standard MDF.
Advantages include:
Higher mechanical strength
Better wear resistance
Improved dimensional stability
Smoother machined edges
Because of its higher density, HDF generally requires:
Higher laser power
Slower cutting speeds
Better smoke extraction
More effective Air Assist
HDF is well suited for products requiring increased durability.
¶ Ultralight MDF
Ultralight MDF is manufactured using lower-density fibers to reduce overall weight.
Advantages include:
Easier cutting
Faster processing
Reduced machine load
Lightweight finished products
However, it may also have:
Lower mechanical strength
Softer edges
Reduced screw-holding capability
Ultralight MDF is commonly used for decorative products and display applications.
¶ Quick Comparison

Laser Processing Suitability

★★★★★ Recommended
